hints: Calculate the work done by the pulling force along the slope: $W_F = F d\cos 20^\circ = 120(5)\cos 20^\circ \approx 563.82\text{ J}$.
Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained: $\Delta E_p = mg d\sin 30^\circ = 10(10)(5)(0.5) = 250\text{ J}$.
Set up the work-energy balance: $W_F - \Delta E_p - W_R = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$, with $W_R = 200\text{ J}$.
Solve $563.82 - 250 - 200 = 5v^2$ to find the final speed $v \approx 4.77\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Name the work-energy principle: the net work done on the block (work done by the applied force minus potential energy gained minus work done against resistance) equals the final kinetic energy gained from rest:
$$W_{\text{applied}} - \Delta E_p - W_{\text{resistance}} = E_k$$

Calculate the work done by the applied force over distance $d = 5\text{ m}$ up the slope, noting the force acts at $20^\circ$ to the slope:
$$W_{\text{applied}} = F d\cos 20^\circ = (120)(5)\cos 20^\circ = 600\cos 20^\circ$$
$$600 \times 0.939693 \approx 563.8156\text{ J}$$

Calculate the increase in gravitational potential energy over the vertical rise $h = 5\sin 30^\circ = 2.5\text{ m}$:
$$\Delta E_p = mgh = (10)(10)(2.5) = 250\text{ J}$$

The work done against resistance is given as $W_{\text{resistance}} = 200\text{ J}$. Form the energy balance:
$$563.8156 - 250 - 200 = \frac{1}{2}(10)v^2$$
$$113.8156 = 5v^2$$

Divide both sides by 5:
$$v^2 = \frac{113.8156}{5} \approx 22.7631$$
$$v = \sqrt{22.7631} \approx 4.7711\text{ m s}^{-1}$$
$$v = 4.77\text{ m s}^{-1}\quad (\text{to 3 significant figures})$$
